shots.name: Shock ring, petal burst, wide arena reveal

camera.where: Field: the player-controlled exploration camera behind the lead hero. On contact the game cuts to authored shots: a tight, low view of the impact point (red shock ring), then a petal-burst wipe, then a wide arena establishing shot from the side (field encounter) or from behind and above the party (boss encounter that follows a cutscene).
camera.height: Impact shot near ground level. Arena shot roughly 1.5 to 2.5 m up, level or tipped slightly down (eyeballed).
camera.distance: Far: the heroes are small in the lower part of the frame and the enemy stands across the arena.
camera.movement: About 3 s of slow-motion sparks on a fixed camera, a petal wipe under 1 s, then a near-static wide shot with a slight push while the heroes run into place, then a motion-blur whip into the first command shot.

shots.frame: Heroes low in frame, enemy across the arena (side-on) or at the top of frame (boss version). The battle HUD fades in during the reveal: enemy name bar first, party HP tiles a beat later, turn-order strip last. No menu until the first actor is up. A 'First Strike!' banner shows when the player opened the fight.
shots.timing: Field first strike: about 3.5 s from impact to the arena wipe, then about 2.5 s of arena before the first menu (FL 1:18 to 1:24.5). Boss fight after a letterboxed cutscene: hard cut to black at 3:57.5, petal burst at 3:57.8, arena lit by 3:59 (about 1.5 s).
shots.whyItWorks: The petal burst repeats the game's Gommage motif, so the swap from field camera to arena camera reads as a designed beat and hides the change of shot. The still wide gives the player the formation before menus arrive [inference]. A reviewer singles out the way each hero swishes into battle.
shots.confidence: [observed: FL 1:18-1:25; FL 3:57-3:59] [single source: Jimquisition, entrance praised] [verified: 2 sources: Xbox Wire tips and the FL 1:25 banner for the First Strike opener]

shots.name: Battle Wheel over the shoulder

camera.where: Behind and slightly to the side of the hero whose turn it is. The hero stands in the left third of the frame with their back turned about 20 to 30 degrees toward the enemy; a second party member is cropped in the right foreground or stands in the right third.
camera.height: About the hero's chest to head height, looking level (eyeballed).
camera.distance: Close: the hero fills roughly half to two thirds of the frame height, about 2 to 3 m away (eyeballed).
camera.movement: Near static with ambient drift (the lead programmer says something is always happening on screen, even in menus). Enters by a whip-pan of under about 0.5 s from the previous shot.

shots.frame: Hero in the left third, enemy in mid-distance centre or right, ally at right. The Battle Wheel hangs in world space off the hero's side as 4 to 5 angled brush-stroke options (Aim, Gradient Attack once charges exist, Items, Skills, Attack) with button glyphs. HUD: turn-order strip of portraits top-left, enemy name and health top-centre, three party HP tiles bottom-right (active one enlarged), Flee and Skip Turn prompts bottom-left, a character-mechanic panel mid-right.
shots.timing: Open-ended hold while the player decides.
shots.whyItWorks: The menu sits inside the picture beside the hero instead of on a separate screen, so the waiting moment is itself a composed frame [inference]. Sandfall names Persona's camera and menus as the model, and critics read the menus as Persona-like.

shots.name: Each skill is a short film

camera.where: Every skill plays its own authored run of 2 to 5 shots: a medium-full shot of the caster (front or three-quarter, low), a close-up with the timing prompt, a whip or push to the enemy for the impact, then a pull-back wide. Some skills use a canted (tilted) frame.
camera.height: Mostly low, from knee to waist height, with some ground-level and overhead shots (eyeballed).
camera.distance: Varies from a face close-up to a full-body medium shot.
camera.movement: Hard cuts, whips with heavy motion blur, camera shake, slow motion on impact and an animated focal length. The menu disappears; the turn-order strip and party tiles stay.

shots.frame: The caster fills the frame with a diamond 'A' prompt and a ring that reads PERFECT when timed well; large world-space damage numbers pop at each hit (24 up to 12,437 seen); a 'Status Effects' tag sits top-right during casts.
shots.timing: About 2 to 5 s per skill: Maelle's Spark runs about 4 s (FL 4:15.2 to 4:19) and Lune's Ice Lance about 3 s (FL 4:33.5 to 4:36). A shot changes about every 1 to 1.5 s.
shots.whyItWorks: Dev intent: each skill is authored in a sequence editor as a small cinematic with camera position, rotation, animated focal length, shakes and time dilation, all for a feeling of intensity. A reviewer credits slow motion and particle flourishes with theatrical drama.

shots.name: Wind-up cutaway before a big attack

camera.where: In the enemy's turn the camera cuts from its wide, low view to an extreme close-up of the enemy charging (IGN clip); for a jump attack it stays low behind the heroes and tilts up to follow the giant out of frame (First Look).
camera.height: Close-up at the enemy's chest and hands; the jump shot at the heroes' knee height, tilting up.
camera.distance: Extreme close-up, or a long low view.
camera.movement: Hard cut in, a slow push during the charge, hard cut back to wide when the strike starts. For jumps a smooth tilt up, then a snap down at impact.

shots.frame: Enemy body fills the frame with its glowing core; the move caption sits top-centre ('Eveque charges up.' or 'Goblu is about to crush Gustave.'); Parry, Dodge and Jump prompts bottom-left; party HP tiles bottom-right.
shots.timing: IGN: close-up from 3:03 to 3:08 (about 5 to 6 s), wide again at 3:09. FL: 'about to crush' caption at 4:45, tilt-up and jump at 4:47, impact at 4:48 (about 3 s of warning).
shots.whyItWorks: The telegraph is also the drama [inference]. Sandfall say camera movement, focal length, shakes and time dilation are used to cue how the player should react, and enemy hit animations are emphasised to nudge the parry. With Camera Movement off, the game itself warns that some attacks become harder to read.

settings.name: Camera Movement (Settings, Accessibility tab)
settings.effect: Default on. Off keeps a wider, stationary battle camera instead of following the action. The in-game text says it primarily affects battle, considerably alters the battle experience and makes some attacks harder to read, and is meant for players who get motion sickness.
settings.source: Can I Play That? (2025-12-04); PC Gamer, Kerry Brunskill (2025-05-08); Linnet's how-to page (game text). [verified: 3 sources]

settings.name: Camera Shake (Accessibility)
settings.effect: Toggles the camera shake effects that add dynamic movement in battle.

settings.name: Automatic QTE (Accessibility)
settings.effect: Own-attack QTEs succeed automatically; dodge and parry are not affected. Not a camera option, but it changes how long the player just watches the execution shots.
settings.source: Linnet's how-to page; RPG Site interview with Meurisse (own-attack QTEs can be disabled); Xbox Wire tips. [verified: 3 sources]

settings.name: Camera sensitivity and invert (Controls)
settings.effect: About 20 steps of sensitivity for the camera stick only, plus inverted axes. Applies to the free camera (exploration and aiming), not the battle camera.

settings.name: Sprint and aim: hold or toggle
settings.effect: Aiming and sprinting can be set to toggle so the trigger need not be held.

settings.name: Field of view
settings.effect: No in-game field-of-view slider; PCGamingWiki points to mods or ReShade.

settings.name: Photo Mode (Thank You Update)
settings.effect: A free camera with unlimited distance that can pass through collisions and works in cinematics. Separate from the battle camera; whether it works mid-battle was not found.
settings.source: expedition33.com dev blog (2026-02-11); PC Gamer, Tyler Wilde (2026-02-11). [verified: 2 sources for what it is; scope in battle not found]

devStatements.who: Guillaume Broche, CEO and creative director
devStatements.summary: Calls Persona 5 the best game in the world for battle depiction and UI, and says he was strongly influenced by the way its camera cuts dramatically each time the player acts, so the fight feels like watching a film. Expedition 33 turns that into camerawork suited to its own game and he says the UI is still being refined. Also lists Final Fantasy VI to X among his influences. Direct quote (Automaton West translation): 'making it feel like you're watching a movie'.
devStatements.source: Denfaminicogamer, 2025-05-23 (Japanese original) https://news.denfaminicogamer.jp/interview/2505223a ; English: Automaton West https://automaton-media.com/en/news/clair-obscur-expedition-33-lead-says-persona-5-is-the-best-game-in-the-world-when-it-comes-to-ui-and-combat-visuals/ and PCGamesN https://www.pcgamesn.com/clair-obscur-expedition-33/persona-5-influence [verified: 3 sources]

devStatements.summary: Says the team studied what Persona did with camera movements, menus and dynamic construction, then did its own version because the art style differs. Says Persona is not the biggest influence: the Final Fantasy VIII, IX and X era shaped much of the game's core, not by direct copying.
devStatements.source: PC Gamer, Robert Jones, 2024-08-28 https://www.pcgamer.com/games/rpg/clair-obscur-expedition-33-creative-director-speaks-candidly-about-the-new-rpgs-respect-for-final-fantasy-and-persona-we-are-definitely-not-hiding-that-there-are-influences/ ; summarised by GamesRadar. [single source, restated by a second outlet]

devStatements.summary: The team loves JRPGs including Final Fantasy, Tales, Lost Odyssey and Persona, and singles out Persona for its UI, rhythm and dynamic camera.

Says Final Fantasy VIII, IX and X shaped many parts of the game, that the sense of a widening world in FF VII to IX became the world map, and that Sekiro influenced the dodge and parry feel. No camera remark.

Calls Final Fantasy X a masterpiece and a big inspiration, specifically for the party, pacing and narrative. Calls Persona 5 a big inspiration for the UI and how dynamic the battles are. Says the turn-based core was influenced by Final Fantasy VIII, IX and X, and that Sekiro pushed the team toward reactive dodging and parrying.
devStatements.source: RPG Site, Adam Vitale and James Galizio, 2025-03-21 https://www.rpgsite.net/interview/17041-clair-obscur-expedition-33-interview-celebrating-turn-based-games-classic-rpg-influences-in-making-something-new [single source]

devStatements.who: Tom Guillermin, co-founder and lead programmer (CTO)
devStatements.summary: Wanted a high level of polish in animation, camera movement and VFX in battle, so that something is always happening even in menus. All skills are treated as small cinematics in Unreal's Sequencer with battle actors bound at runtime, which gives flexibility to create epic shots. Arenas are controlled environments; level designers can adjust enemy positions case by case, and dynamic moves such as an enemy jumping at a hero from any position are handled by exposing properties to the sequence and keyframing them. Direct quote: 'treating all skills as small cinematics'.
devStatements.source: Unreal Engine developer interview, 2025-03-27 (read via Internet Archive; direct fetch returned 403) https://web.archive.org/web/20260420221013/https://www.unrealengine.com/developer-interviews/inside-the-development-journey-of-clair-obscur-expedition-33 [single source]

devStatements.who: Tom Guillermin (with Florian Torres, GDC 2026 talk)
devStatements.summary: A skill is authored end to end in Blueprints: character movement, visual effects and camera movement. You control the camera's location and rotation and its focal length, which can be animated, plus camera shakes, VFX and time dilation, all adding to a feeling of intensity over the course of the skill.

devStatements.who: Michel Nohra, lead game designer (MIGS 2025 talk, reported by MobileSyrup)
devStatements.summary: The animation team uses time dilation, focal length, camera shakes and camera movement to punctuate important moments and to cue how players should react; enemy hit animations are emphasised in the enemy turn to nudge the parry. The victory screen was built around a juicy freeze frame.
devStatements.source: MobileSyrup, Katya Ryabova, 2025-11-27 https://mobilesyrup.com/2025/11/27/clair-obscur-expedition-33-devs-combat-hard-juicy/ [single source, second-hand report of a talk]

devStatements.who: Finding: Final Fantasy X and the battle camera
devStatements.summary: No source found in which Sandfall says its battle camera drew on Final Fantasy X. FFX is credited for party, pacing and narrative (Meurisse), and with FF VIII and IX for the turn-based core (Meurisse, Broche). The camera lineage they name is Persona 5. [not found]
devStatements.source: See the Meurisse, Broche and Guillermin entries above.
